references.text: At Jesus' baptism, the Father's voice sounds from heaven and calls Jesus "my Son, the beloved" – the same expression the owner of the vineyard uses for his son in the parable: "my son, the beloved" (τὸν υἱόν μου τὸν ἀγαπητόν). See [ref:Luk 3:22|Luke 3:22].

At the transfiguration on the mountain, God calls Jesus "my chosen Son" / "my beloved Son." This connects to the vineyard owner's reference to his son as "my beloved son." See [ref:Luk 9:35|Luke 9:35].
Mark's parallel to the parable uses a similar formulation: the owner still had one left, his beloved son, and finally sent him. See [ref:Mark 12:6|Mark 12:6].
Matthew's parallel: Finally, the owner sent his son to the tenants and said, "They will respect my son." See [ref:Matt 21:37|Matthew 21:37].

In these last days God has spoken to us through the Son, after having spoken through the prophets (the servants). This corresponds to the pattern in the parable where the lord first sent servants and finally sent his son. See [ref:Hebr 1:1-2|Hebrews 1:1-2].
God sent his only begotten Son into the world – this reflects the vineyard owner's decision to send his beloved son as the final and decisive messenger. See [ref:Joh 3:16-17|John 3:16-17].

Paul writes that when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son. The fact that God "sends" the Son after having sent the prophets corresponds to the pattern in the parable. See [ref:Gal 4:4|Galatians 4:4].
God's love was revealed by sending his only begotten Son into the world. The motif of sending the beloved son is central in the parable. See [ref:1 Joh 4:9-10|1 John 4:9-10].
Isaiah's song about the vineyard forms the background for the parable of the vineyard and its owner. The lord expects fruit from the vineyard but is disappointed. See [ref:Jes 5:1-5|Isaiah 5:1-5].
